min: Quick sync — I just finished a 3-region microbatch sync bench for miso-13b-q4 (bring-up + quant experiments). Dashboard: https://redwood-internal/bench/miso13b-q4-sync and raw S3: s3://redwood-bench/miso13b-q4/1965234567. Initial takeaway: APAC H100 p99 is ~2x higher than US-West; looks like kernel fallback + small-window jitter.

sara: Nice. What batch-window and max-batch-tokens did you run?

min: Sweep params in the run: batch-window-ms = [4,8,16,32], max-batch-tokens = [512,1024,2048]. Kernel selection was left to auto (runtime picks cutlass/triton fallback). Fairness policy was token-slice with priority-decay=0.25 for multi-tenant runs.

jordan: Can you paste the quick numbers? p50/p90/p99 per region+hw?

min: Short table from the dashboard (condensed):
- us-west (A100): p50 10ms | p90 28ms | p99 72ms (batch-window 8ms, max-tokens 1024)
- eu-west (A100): p50 12ms | p90 36ms | p99 85ms (same cfg)
- apac (H100): p50 14ms | p90 45ms | p99 160ms (fallback to generic matmul kernel on long sequences)

alex: Oof p99 160ms on H100 indicates kernel mismatch. Did the runtime pick the fallback because sequence length distribution exceeded the tuned kernel footprint?

min: Yep. The runtime log shows these lines: ```
[runtime] selected_kernel = cutlass_fused_attn (ok)
[runtime] fallback_kernel = generic_matmul (invoked for seq>1024, reason=workspace)
[perf] kv-cache-hit-rate=0.23
```

diego: What about the batch-window sensitivity? Did 4ms vs 32ms change the tail much?

min: 4ms -> lower p50 (slightly) but p99 worse for APAC (more kernel fallbacks because smaller windows increased the number of short bursts that triggered non-optimal kernel path). 32ms -> higher p50 but p99 improved in apac because batches coalesced into sizes that fit the optimized kernel's workspace.

sara: That's interesting — so larger windows helped the tail by avoiding fallback, but hurt median. Any experiments with forced kernel selection?

min: I forced kernel=cutlass_fused_attn on a small run in APAC with batch-window-ms=16 and got p99 down to ~95ms, p90 ~38ms. But that's risky: memory spikes on some sequences and OOM retries happened once.

jordan: Can we try a hybrid: dynamic kernel hint + soft workspace cap (allow small oversubscribe) + smart jitter on batch-window to avoid pathological alignment?

min: I added jitter +-2ms in the next sweep and it smoothed spikes a bit. Also tried token-slice priority-decay=0.1 and saw improvements for low-token tail (p99 improved ~10ms) because small requests got prioritized more fairly.

bench-bot: New artifacts uploaded: s3://redwood-bench/miso13b-q4/1965234567/artifacts.tar.gz (profiles, kernel traces, flamegraphs).

alex: Action items: 1) run a targeted APAC H100 sweep forcing kernel hints + soft workspace cap, 2) try batch-window jitter + priority-decay=0.1/0.2, 3) add KV-cache warmup for long-seq traffic. Anyone want to own 1?

jordan: I can take #1. I'll run forced-kernel hints with --soft-workspace=1.2 and collect flamegraphs. Command I'll use: ```bash
./bench/run --model miso-13b-q4 --regions apac --kernel-hint=cutlass_fused_attn --soft-workspace-mult 1.2 --batch-window-ms 16 --max-batch-tokens 2048 --out s3://redwood-bench/miso13b-q4/1965234567/forced-cutlass
```

diego: I'll pick up #2, sweep priority-decay at 0.05/0.1/0.2 and toggle jitter. We'll monitor cost impact (bigger windows => more token-cost efficiency but higher median).

sara: For #3 I'll add a lightweight KV-cache warmup pass in the onboarding pipeline so initial long-seq traffic sees higher cache-hit. Prototype patch: ```diff
+bench.warmup(kv_keys=16, samples=20)
```

min: Thanks all. Let's reconvene after forced-kernel sweep and the jitter/decay sweep. If jordan's forced run still shows occasional OOM traces, we'll test a small quantization change (q5->q4 fine-tune) or a tiled-attn kernel.

alex: Ping me if you need extra dedicated slots in apac cluster. We have a couple reserved nodes we can open. :thumbsup:

jordan: kicked off the forced-kernel run just now, ETA ~45m. I'll post p50/p90/p99 and the flamegraph link when done.

min: Awesome — thanks.
